questions.q: A "model" that is just a lookup table scores 100% on the customers it was trained on. What does this tell you about its performance on new customers?
options: It will also be close to 100%
It proves the features are well chosen
It will be exactly 50%
Almost nothing: it may simply have memorised the answers, so only data it has never seen can show how well it generalises
questions.why: A flexible model can memorise its examples, so a training score measures recall, not generalisation. Assuming a perfect training score carries over to new data is the very trap that a held-out test set exists to catch.

questions.q: A dataset has 25,000 rows, of which 4% are defaults. With a stratified 80/20 split, how many defaults are in the test set?
questions.why: The test set has 20% of 25,000 = 5,000 rows, and stratifying keeps the 4% rate: 0.04 × 5,000 = **200**. 1,000 is all the defaults in the whole dataset; 800 is how many land in the training set.

questions.q: A classifier is 90% accurate on 400 test rows. Using SE = √(p(1 − p) / n), what is the approximate 95% margin (1.96 × SE)?
options: About ±0.2 points
About ±2.9 points
About ±9 points
About ±1.5 points
questions.why: SE = √(0.9 × 0.1 / 400) = √0.000225 = 0.015, and 1.96 × 0.015 ≈ 0.029, so about **±2.9 percentage points**. ±1.5 points is one standard error, not the 95% margin; ±9 points forgets the square root.

questions.q: On the same 200 test rows, Model A scores 84% accuracy and Model B scores 86%. How should you read this?
options: B is clearly better and should be deployed
The gap is well inside the roughly ±4.9-point uncertainty of a 200-row test set, so the scores cannot really separate the models
A is better because it is more conservative
The test set is too large to be useful
questions.why: A test score is an estimate with uncertainty: at 85% on 200 rows, 1.96 × SE is about ±4.9 points. A 2-point gap is easily luck. Treating every difference in test scores as real is the misconception; use more test rows or cross-validation to separate them.

questions.q: You compared three models on a validation set and picked the best one. What is the correct next step?
options: Report the best validation score as the final result
Try more models on the test set until one beats the validation score
Retrain the chosen model on training plus validation data, then score it once on the untouched test set and report that
Discard the test set because validation was enough
questions.why: Choosing among models is itself a kind of learning, so the winning validation score is slightly optimistic. Reporting it directly is the tempting shortcut; the honest number is a single score on data used neither for training nor for choosing.

questions.q: A demand forecast scores an MAE of 50 units with a random split and 80 units when trained on earlier months and tested on later ones. Which number should you report, and why?
options: 80, because the time-based split copies reality: on the day the model is used, only the past is available
50, because it is the better score
The average, 65
Neither; time-series models cannot be evaluated
questions.why: A random split lets the model learn from months after the one it predicts, so patterns such as a festive surge leak across the split. The worse, time-based number is the true one. Preferring the better-looking score is exactly how leakage goes unnoticed.

questions.q: You expect about 80% accuracy and want the 95% margin (1.96 × SE) to be no more than ±2 percentage points. Roughly how many test rows do you need?
options: About 1,540
About 800
About 400
About 16,000
questions.why: Solve 1.96 × √(0.8 × 0.2 / n) ≤ 0.02: n ≥ 1.96² × 0.16 / 0.02² ≈ 1,537, so about **1,540** rows. About 400 forgets to square 1.96; 16,000 squares the margin as if it were 0.002 rather than 0.02 (wrong units).

questions.q: Interview: "Your model will score customers it has never seen, and each customer has many rows of history. How do you split?" Which answer is best?
options: A plain random split of rows, because shuffling removes all bias
Put the largest customers in the test set
Use the same customers in train and test but different columns
Split by customer (a group split), so every row of a test customer is unseen; the test set must look like tomorrow, which here means new customers
questions.why: With a row-level random split, the same customer appears on both sides and the model is partly tested on people it already knows, which flatters the score. The guiding question is: what will be different on the day the model is used? Here, the customers.
